animation.note: The earliest documented start of an infantry brigade is Armistead's brigade at 3 a.m. from a bivouac about four miles out on the Chambersburg turnpike; 03:00 is the start of a march from off the field, not a presence on it (the Q04 floor of 04:36 applies to presence on the scene, so the viewer draws the march from off the field first and the brigade on the field only from 04:36; Dearing's battalion, documented on the field at dusk of 2 July, is the earliest part of the division present); it is drawn as a march, not a spawn. No report times its arrival on the field; Garnett's brigade reached the field about 9 a.m. The later readings stay selectable. This bears on gate Q04, which keeps the division off the scene until sunrise (04:36): see the readers.

default.note: The record gives brigade times, not a division time: the morning is certain, the hour is not. Dearing's guns were on the field at dusk of the 2d.

weighing.summary: Two questions were run together. Date: the division came within about three or four miles of Gettysburg on the afternoon of 2 Jul (Lee 1864, Alexander, Hoke, Aylett, Dearing) and spent the night there; it did not reach the field that night except Dearing's guns, which moved up at dusk. On the field: the infantry brigades went in on the morning of 3 Jul (Lee 1863: joined Longstreet the following morning; Aylett: Armistead's brigade moved at 3 a.m.; Peyton: Garnett's brigade reached the field about 9 a.m.; Fremantle, Dickert and Owen: just come up). The values that look opposed (night of the 2d, afternoon of the 2d, the 3rd) are different events: arrival in the neighbourhood, the guns at dusk, the infantry on the field. No source gives 06:00 on the 2d. No order to Pickett is in the record. The default is the plan's own morning of Jul 3, with the brigade hours it rests on.
weighing.who: Aylett commanded Armistead's brigade, Peyton Garnett's brigade and Dearing the artillery battalion attached to the division: all three were with the units they describe. Lee commanded the army and ordered the division forward. Fremantle, Dickert, Owen and Wilcox saw the division on the ridge but not its march. Alexander, Hoke, Toombs, Hunt and the Park Service handbook were not with it. No report of Pickett, Kemper or Garnett exists (Garnett was killed and Kemper wounded, Fremantle and Lee's report; Lee asked Pickett to modify his and he did not, Alexander 1907).
weighing.when: Peyton wrote on 9 Jul, Aylett on 12 Jul, Lee on 31 Jul 1863, Dearing on 16 Aug 1863 (days to six weeks after); Lee's detailed report is of Jan 1864. Hunt (1887), Hoke (1887), Toombs (1888), Longstreet (1896), Taylor (1906) and Alexander (1907) are 24 to 44 years later; the Park Service handbook is of 1954. The reports of 1863 outrank the memoirs and the books.
weighing.where: Aylett was with Armistead's brigade on the turnpike four miles out and then on the field; Peyton with Garnett's brigade; Dearing with the guns, which went up at dusk. Lee, at his headquarters, wrote of the three brigades together. Fremantle was on the ridge from 6 a.m. on the 3d.
weighing.how_knew: Aylett, Peyton and Dearing give the hours of their own commands and say how (moved at 3 a.m.; reached the field about 9 a.m.; orders received about dusk). Lee had it from reports. Alexander, Hoke, Toombs, Hunt and the handbook give no source; W. M. Owen compiled his book of 1885 from his diary; Captain H. T. Owen (1881) wrote as an officer of Garnett's brigade.
weighing.clock: Every writer is Confederate or unspecified; the Confederate hours (3 a.m., 9 a.m., about dusk) are not corrected for the reported 20-minute difference between the armies' clocks, which would not change a morning or an afternoon. 'About 9' keeps a quarter hour either way.
weighing.independence: The default rests on the separate reports of two brigades (Aylett, Peyton), the artillery battalion (Dearing) and Lee, with Fremantle, Dickert, Owen and Wilcox as witnesses on the ridge that morning; they are independent of each other. Lee 1863 and Lee 1864 are one writer. Hoke is only the carrier of Captain H. T. Owen's article of 1881; Toombs, Hunt and the handbook name no source.

source_panel_text: The morning of Jul 3: Armistead's brigade left its camp four miles out at 3 a.m. and Garnett's brigade reached the field about 9 a.m. (reports of July 1863); Lee has the brigades joining Longstreet that morning. On Jul 2 they were only near the field, apart from the artillery at dusk. Ten other values are listed.
